title: Game Theory
description: Your best move depends on what everyone else decides to do.
attribution: von Neumann, Morgenstern, Nash and others
takeaway: Ask what each participant wants and how they can respond.

blocks.text: Some choices cannot be understood in isolation. A café choosing a price, for example, may care about the price chosen by another café. Each decision changes the setting in which the other decision makes sense. Game theory gives a mathematical language for these interactions.

A model identifies players, available actions, and outcomes those players value. It can describe competition, cooperation, or a mixture of both. The word game does not require a board or a winner who takes everything.

The value of the model depends on its assumptions. It should represent the incentives and responses that matter for the question. Leaving out something a participant values can change what looks like a sensible choice.

details.title: When no one gains by changing alone

blocks.text: A Nash equilibrium is a collection of strategies in which no player can improve their own payoff by changing alone while the others keep their strategies fixed. It describes a particular kind of stability in the model, rather than a promise of a desirable result.

Nash established equilibrium existence for finite games when mixed strategies are allowed. A mixed strategy randomizes over available actions. Allowing this possibility changes the mathematical question from finding a fixed action for every player to finding strategies that may include probabilities.

An equilibrium need not be fair, efficient, unique, or easy to reach. The definition asks about an individual departure from the current strategies, not whether a coordinated change could make everyone better off.

Imagine two cafés choosing prices. List their choices and valued outcomes, then ask how each would respond while the other’s choice stays fixed. A tempting move may look different once responses matter.
This organizes a question rather than predicting actual cafés. People can lack information, act inconsistently, or value relationships a small payoff table leaves out.

items: Name the players and their choices.
State what each participant actually values.
Individual stability need not mean collective benefit.

blocks.text: Each café’s result depends on its own choice and its rival’s choice. Before asking for the best move, build a picture of the interaction. A move is strategic because someone else can respond, not simply because it sounds clever.

items: Consider their best responses to one another.

blocks.text: A small strategic model can reveal an overlooked response. It can also hide something important behind a convenient assumption. Before carrying its conclusion into the world, inspect what it leaves out and how the outcome might change if that assumption changed.
Keep in mind: real people may lack information or value things the model omits.

items: What would the other player do next?
What does each participant actually care about?
Could a coordinated change differ from a change made alone?
